place-value.base-ten.name: A ten is a bundle of ten ones
place-value.base-ten.statement: Ten ones grouped together form one unit called a ten, and the numeral 10 represents one ten and no ones.

place-value.base-ten.name: The two digits of a two-digit number are tens and ones
place-value.base-ten.statement: In a two-digit numeral, the left digit counts tens and the right digit counts ones, so the number is that many tens plus that many ones (47 is 4 tens and 7 ones, 40 + 7).

place-value.base-ten.name: A hundred is a bundle of ten tens
place-value.base-ten.statement: Ten tens grouped together form one unit called a hundred, equal to one hundred ones.

place-value.base-ten.name: The three digits of a three-digit number are hundreds, tens, and ones
place-value.base-ten.statement: In a three-digit numeral, the digits from left to right count hundreds, tens, and ones, so the number is that many hundreds plus tens plus ones (706 is 7 hundreds, 0 tens, and 6 ones).

place-value.base-ten.name: Each whole-number place is ten times the place to its right
place-value.base-ten.statement: In a multi-digit whole number, a digit in one place represents ten times what the same digit represents in the place to its right.

place-value.base-ten.name: Move between a whole-number numeral and its expanded form
place-value.base-ten.statement: A whole number up to 1,000,000 is the sum of the values of its digits, and expanded form writes that sum with one term per nonzero digit (40,603 = 40,000 + 600 + 3).

multiplication.properties.name: The commutative property of multiplication
multiplication.properties.statement: For any numbers a and b, a x b = b x a.

multiplication.properties.name: The associative property of multiplication
multiplication.properties.statement: For any numbers a, b and c, (a x b) x c = a x (b x c): when three numbers are multiplied, the product does not depend on which adjacent pair is multiplied first.

multiplication.properties.name: The distributive property of multiplication over addition
multiplication.properties.statement: For any numbers a, b and c, a x (b + c) = a x b + a x c.

multiplication.properties.name: Multiplying by 1 leaves a number unchanged
multiplication.properties.statement: For any number a, a x 1 = a and 1 x a = a.

multiplication.properties.name: Multiplying by 0 gives 0
multiplication.properties.statement: For any number a, a x 0 = 0 and 0 x a = 0.

factors-multiples.whole-number.name: A factor pair of a whole number
factors-multiples.whole-number.statement: A factor pair of a whole number n is two whole numbers whose product is n; each is a factor of n.

factors-multiples.whole-number.name: Find all factor pairs of a whole number within 100
factors-multiples.whole-number.statement: List every factor pair of a whole number n from 1 to 100 by testing each whole number d from 1 upward as a factor, stopping once d x d is greater than n, because in every pair the smaller factor d has d x d no greater than n.

factors-multiples.whole-number.name: A whole number is a multiple of each of its factors
factors-multiples.whole-number.statement: If d is a factor of n, then n is a multiple of d: n = d x k for a whole number k, so n is in the list d, 2 x d, 3 x d, ...

factors-multiples.whole-number.name: Decide whether a whole number within 100 is a multiple of a one-digit number
factors-multiples.whole-number.statement: A whole number n from 1 to 100 is a multiple of a one-digit number d exactly when d x k = n for some whole number k, which is checked by skip-counting by d or by dividing n by d and looking for a remainder of 0.

factors-multiples.whole-number.name: Prime and composite numbers
factors-multiples.whole-number.statement: A whole number greater than 1 is prime if its only factors are 1 and itself, and composite if it has a factor other than 1 and itself; 1 is neither prime nor composite.

factors-multiples.whole-number.name: Decide whether a whole number within 100 is prime or composite
factors-multiples.whole-number.statement: A whole number from 2 to 100 is composite if it is a multiple of some number from 2 to 9 other than itself, and prime otherwise, because any factor pair of a number up to 100 contains a factor no greater than 10.

addition.whole-number.name: Add like base-ten units
addition.whole-number.statement: Adding two numbers written in base ten means adding hundreds to hundreds, tens to tens, and ones to ones; units of different sizes are never combined directly.

addition.whole-number.name: Compose a ten or a hundred when adding
addition.whole-number.statement: Ten ones make one ten and ten tens make one hundred, so when the units of one place total 10 or more, 10 of them can be traded for 1 unit of the next larger place without changing the number.

addition.whole-number.name: Add within 1000 with base-ten models
addition.whole-number.statement: Find a sum within 1000 with base-ten blocks or a drawing by joining like units and trading 10 ones for a ten and 10 tens for a hundred where needed.

addition.whole-number.name: Add within 1000 by partial sums, without a model
addition.whole-number.statement: Add two to four numbers within 1000, without blocks or drawings, by adding the hundreds, the tens, and the ones separately and then combining the partial sums.

addition.whole-number.name: Relate a base-ten addition model to a written method
addition.whole-number.statement: Each step of a base-ten model of an addition matches a part of a written method in columns: joining like units matches adding a column, and each trade of 10 units for 1 of the next place matches a carried 1.

addition.whole-number.name: Explain a place-value addition strategy with properties
addition.whole-number.statement: Adding by place value gives the correct sum because splitting the addends into place-value parts and regrouping those parts uses only the commutative and associative properties of addition, which never change a sum.

addition.whole-number.name: Add multi-digit whole numbers with the standard algorithm
addition.whole-number.statement: Add multi-digit whole numbers by adding column by column from the ones, writing each column's ones digit and carrying its tens digit to the next column left.

addition.whole-number.name: Add within 10 fluently
addition.whole-number.statement: Give any sum of two whole numbers with a total of 10 or less quickly and accurately, without counting.

addition.whole-number.name: Know all sums of two one-digit numbers
addition.whole-number.statement: Give any sum of two one-digit numbers, including those greater than 10, quickly and accurately without counting.

subtraction.whole-number.name: Subtract like base-ten units
subtraction.whole-number.statement: Subtracting numbers written in base ten means subtracting hundreds from hundreds, tens from tens, and ones from ones; units of different sizes are never subtracted from each other directly.

subtraction.whole-number.name: Decompose a ten or a hundred when subtracting
subtraction.whole-number.statement: When a place has too few units to subtract from, 1 unit of the next larger place can be traded for 10 units of this place without changing the number.

subtraction.whole-number.name: Subtract within 1000 with base-ten models
subtraction.whole-number.statement: Find a difference within 1000 with base-ten blocks or a drawing by taking away like units, trading 1 ten for 10 ones or 1 hundred for 10 tens where needed.

subtraction.whole-number.name: Subtract within 1000 by taking away place-value parts, without a model
subtraction.whole-number.statement: Subtract within 1000, without blocks or drawings, by taking away the subtrahend's hundreds, then its tens, then its ones, one part at a time.

subtraction.whole-number.name: Subtract within 1000 by adding up from the subtrahend
subtraction.whole-number.statement: Find a - b, without blocks or drawings, as the missing addend in b + ? = a by adding up from b to a in place-value jumps (to the next ten, the next hundred, then on to a) and totaling the jumps.

subtraction.whole-number.name: Relate a base-ten subtraction model to a written method
subtraction.whole-number.statement: Each step of a base-ten model of a subtraction matches a part of a written method in columns: taking away like units matches subtracting a column, and each trade of 1 unit for 10 of the next smaller place matches crossing out a digit, writing it 1 less, and adding 10 to the place on its right.

subtraction.whole-number.name: Explain a place-value subtraction strategy with properties
subtraction.whole-number.statement: Taking away a number in place-value parts gives the correct difference because taking away b + c is the same as taking away b and then c: a - (b + c) = (a - b) - c.

subtraction.whole-number.name: Subtract multi-digit whole numbers with the standard algorithm
subtraction.whole-number.statement: Subtract a whole number from a larger or equal one column by column from the ones, regrouping from the nearest nonzero place to the left whenever a top digit is smaller than the digit below it.

subtraction.whole-number.name: Subtract within 10 fluently
subtraction.whole-number.statement: Give any difference a - b with a at most 10 and b at most a quickly and accurately, without counting.

subtraction.whole-number.name: Subtract within 20 fluently
subtraction.whole-number.statement: Give any difference a - b in which b and a - b are both one-digit numbers (so a is at most 18), including those that cross 10, quickly and accurately without counting.

multiplication.multi-digit.name: Multiply a one-digit number by a multiple of 10, 100, or 1000
multiplication.multi-digit.statement: Multiply a one-digit number by a one-digit multiple of a base-ten unit by multiplying the one-digit numbers and keeping the unit: 9 x 80 = 9 x 8 tens = 72 tens = 720.

multiplication.multi-digit.name: Multiply a multiple of 10 by a multiple of 10
multiplication.multi-digit.statement: A product of two multiples of 10 such as 30 x 40 equals (3 x 4) x (10 x 10), so it is that many hundreds: 30 x 40 = 12 hundreds = 1200.

multiplication.multi-digit.name: Multiply a multi-digit number by a one-digit number with partial products
multiplication.multi-digit.statement: Multiply a whole number of up to four digits by a one-digit number by splitting the multi-digit factor into place-value parts, multiplying each part by the one-digit factor, and adding the partial products (the distributive property).

multiplication.multi-digit.name: Multiply two two-digit numbers with partial products
multiplication.multi-digit.statement: Multiply two two-digit numbers by splitting both into tens and ones, finding the four products of a part of one factor with a part of the other, and adding them.

multiplication.multi-digit.name: Multiply multi-digit whole numbers with the standard algorithm
multiplication.multi-digit.statement: Multiply multi-digit whole numbers by finding, for each digit of one factor, a shifted row that multiplies the other factor by that digit with carrying, and adding the rows.

multiplication.multi-digit.name: Recall all products of two one-digit numbers
multiplication.multi-digit.statement: The product of any two one-digit numbers is known from memory, without counting or computing.

division.multi-digit.name: Divide by a one-digit number with partial quotients, no remainder
division.multi-digit.statement: Find the whole-number quotient of a dividend of up to four digits by a one-digit divisor, when it divides exactly, by repeatedly subtracting easy multiples of the divisor (such as 100 or 10 times it) and adding up how many divisors were subtracted.

division.multi-digit.name: Find a quotient and remainder for a one-digit divisor with partial quotients
division.multi-digit.statement: When a one-digit divisor does not divide a dividend of up to four digits exactly, partial quotients stop when the amount left is less than the divisor; the sum of the partial quotients is the whole-number quotient q and the amount left is the remainder r, with dividend = q x divisor + r and r less than the divisor.

division.multi-digit.name: Divide by a two-digit number with partial quotients
division.multi-digit.statement: Find the whole-number quotient (and remainder, if any) of a dividend of up to four digits by a two-digit divisor by partial quotients, estimating each multiple of the divisor to subtract and choosing a smaller one when the estimate is more than the amount left.

division.multi-digit.name: Recall division facts within 100
division.multi-digit.statement: Recall the quotient of a divided by b whenever a = b x c with b and c whole numbers from 1 to 10.

decimal.operations.name: Add decimals to hundredths with a place-value model
decimal.operations.statement: Find a sum of decimals to hundredths with base-ten blocks or grids by joining like units (ones, tenths, hundredths) and trading 10 hundredths for 1 tenth and 10 tenths for 1 one where needed.

decimal.operations.name: Subtract decimals to hundredths with a place-value model
decimal.operations.statement: Find a difference of decimals to hundredths with base-ten blocks or grids by taking away like units, trading 1 tenth for 10 hundredths or 1 one for 10 tenths where needed.

decimal.operations.name: Multiply a decimal by a whole number with a place-value model
decimal.operations.statement: Find n x d, for a whole number n and a decimal d to hundredths, by making n copies of d with blocks or grids, combining like units, and trading 10 hundredths for 1 tenth and 10 tenths for 1 one.

decimal.operations.name: Multiply two decimals with an area model
decimal.operations.statement: Find the product of two decimals, with a product to hundredths, as the area of a rectangle with those side lengths on a grid where the unit square is split into 100 hundredths, so a tenth times a tenth is one hundredth.

decimal.operations.name: Divide a decimal by a whole number with a place-value model
decimal.operations.statement: Find d divided by n, for a decimal d to hundredths and a one-digit whole number n with a quotient to hundredths, by sharing the blocks for d into n equal groups, trading 1 one for 10 tenths or 1 tenth for 10 hundredths when a unit cannot be shared evenly.

decimal.operations.name: Divide by a decimal with a model, as how many groups
decimal.operations.statement: Find a divided by d, for a decimal divisor d in tenths or hundredths with a whole-number quotient, by finding how many copies of d make a on a model.

decimal.operations.name: Relate a decimal addition model to a written method
decimal.operations.statement: Lining up the decimal points in a written decimal sum puts like units (ones, tenths, hundredths) in the same column, matching the joining of like units in the model; each trade of 10 units for 1 of the next place matches a carried 1.

decimal.operations.name: Relate a decimal subtraction model to a written method
decimal.operations.statement: Lining up the decimal points in a written decimal difference puts like units in the same column, matching taking away like units in the model; each trade of 1 unit for 10 of the next smaller place matches regrouping in the written columns.

decimal.operations.name: Relate decimal multiplication models to the decimal-point rule
decimal.operations.statement: In an area model, a tenth times a tenth is a hundredth, so a product of a factor in tenths and a factor in tenths is a whole number of hundredths; this matches the written method of multiplying as whole numbers and giving the product as many decimal places as the factors have together.

decimal.operations.name: Relate decimal division models to a written method
decimal.operations.statement: Sharing a decimal in a model, trading leftover ones for tenths and leftover tenths for hundredths, matches written long division where the decimal point of the quotient is placed directly above the decimal point of the dividend and each leftover is brought down into the next smaller place.

r1.statement: The sum a + b is shown on a number line by placing a length of b units end to end after the length from 0 to a; the endpoint is a + b.
procedure: Mark the length from 0 to a.
From a, mark a further length of b units to the right, in one jump or in smaller jumps that total b.
Read the label at the endpoint; it is a + b.
r1.assess: Show 38 + 25 on a number line and find the sum.
r1.why: The model must represent the meaning of a + b as the total from joining a and b, and the endpoint is read as the sum.

r2.statement: A fraction with denominator 100 is written in decimal notation with whole ones before the point and the remaining hundredths in two places after the point, using a 0 in the tenths place when there are fewer than 10 hundredths (62/100 = 0.62, 5/100 = 0.05).
r2.why: The second place after the point is a further place-value position worth one hundredth.

r3.statement: A fraction with denominator 10 is written in decimal notation with its number of tenths shown as whole ones before the point and the remaining tenths in the first place after the point (3/10 = 0.3, 14/10 = 1.4).
r3.why: The first place after the point is a new place-value position worth one tenth, extending base-ten place value.

r4.statement: A fraction with denominator 10 is written in decimal notation with its number of tenths shown as whole ones before the point and the remaining tenths in the first place after the point (3/10 = 0.3, 14/10 = 1.4).
r4.why: The first place after the point is a new place-value position worth one tenth, extending base-ten place value.

r5.statement: When a objects are put into equal groups of b objects each, the quotient a divided by b is the number of groups.
r5.assess: 24 stickers are put into packs of 6, and 24 divided by 6 is 4. What does the 4 tell you?
r5.why: Alternative route proposed by the critic: Repeated-removal route: take groups of b from a until none remain and count the groups, with no multiplication.

r6.statement: Compute (1/b) divided by a whole number n greater than 0 by multiplying the denominator b by n.
procedure: Multiply the denominator b by the divisor n.
Write the quotient as 1/(b x n).
r6.why: Step 1 multiplies the denominator b by the divisor n, which may be multi-digit.

r7.statement: For whole numbers a and b, with b not 0 and a a multiple of b, a divided by b is the whole number c for which b x c = a.
r7.assess: Which multiplication fact shows that 42 divided by 7 is 6?
r7.why: Turning c groups of b into the equation b x c = a uses the commutative property of multiplication.

r8.statement: Compute a whole number n divided by a unit fraction 1/b by multiplying n by b.
procedure: Multiply the whole number n by the denominator b of the unit fraction.
Write n x b as the quotient.
r8.why: Step 1 multiplies the whole number n by the denominator b, which may be multi-digit.

r9.statement: Adding two fractions means joining their parts into one amount, where both fractions refer to the same whole.
r9.assess: Using one bar as the whole, draw what 2/5 + 1/5 means and say what the sum counts.
r9.why: Adding fractions as joining extends the meaning of whole-number addition as putting two amounts together.

r10.statement: For fractions with the same denominator, a/b + c/b = (a + c)/b.
procedure: Check that the denominators are the same.
Add the numerators.
Write the sum over the common denominator.
r10.why: Step 2 adds the two numerators as whole numbers, possibly with several digits.

r11.statement: For fractions with the same denominator, a/b + c/b = (a + c)/b.
procedure: Check that the denominators are the same.
Add the numerators.
Write the sum over the common denominator.
r11.why: Step 2 adds the two numerators as whole numbers, possibly with several digits.

r12.statement: Add a/b + c/d by rewriting both fractions over a common multiple n of b and d (b x d always works), then adding the numerators over n.
procedure: Find a common multiple n of the denominators b and d (b x d is always one).
Rewrite a/b as (a x (n/b))/n and c/d as (c x (n/d))/n.
Add the two numerators and write the sum over n.
r12.why: Step 1 finds a common multiple n of the two denominators b and d.

r13.statement: Add a/b + c/d by rewriting both fractions over a common multiple n of b and d (b x d always works), then adding the numerators over n.
procedure: Find a common multiple n of the denominators b and d (b x d is always one).
Rewrite a/b as (a x (n/b))/n and c/d as (c x (n/d))/n.
Add the two numerators and write the sum over n.
r13.why: Step 2 computes the multiplier n/b and n/d, which are whole-number quotients of the common multiple by each denominator.

r14.statement: Add a/b + c/d by rewriting both fractions over a common multiple n of b and d (b x d always works), then adding the numerators over n.
procedure: Find a common multiple n of the denominators b and d (b x d is always one).
Rewrite a/b as (a x (n/b))/n and c/d as (c x (n/d))/n.
Add the two numerators and write the sum over n.
r14.why: Alternative route proposed by the critic: Take n = b x d as the common multiple, so the multipliers are d and b and no division or multiples analysis is needed.

r15.statement: A story divides a whole number of units equally into a whole number of shares where the answer is not a whole number; the learner writes the quotient as a fraction or mixed number.
r15.assess: 9 people share a 50-pound sack of rice equally by weight. How many pounds does each person get, and between what two whole numbers does the answer lie?
r15.why: Writing 50/9 as a mixed number needs division with a remainder; the only proposed edge to it is via the between-whole-numbers node, which is task-only here.

r16.statement: For a fraction a/b, divide a by b with remainder to get quotient q and remainder r; if r = 0 then a/b equals the whole number q, otherwise a/b lies strictly between q and q + 1.
procedure: Divide a by b to get a whole-number quotient q and remainder r.
If r = 0, a/b equals the whole number q.
Otherwise, a/b lies between the whole numbers q and q + 1.
r16.assess: Between which two whole numbers does 47/6 lie?
r16.why: Step 1 divides a by b with a remainder to get the quotient q and remainder r.

r17.statement: For a fraction a/b, divide a by b with remainder to get quotient q and remainder r; if r = 0 then a/b equals the whole number q, otherwise a/b lies strictly between q and q + 1.
procedure: Divide a by b to get a whole-number quotient q and remainder r.
If r = 0, a/b equals the whole number q.
Otherwise, a/b lies between the whole numbers q and q + 1.
r17.assess: Between which two whole numbers does 47/6 lie?
r17.why: Step 1 divides a by b with a remainder to get the quotient q and remainder r.

r18.statement: Compare two fractions by rewriting both over a common denominator with the multiplication principle; the fraction with the greater rewritten numerator is greater.
procedure: Find a common multiple of the two denominators (the product of the denominators always works).
Rewrite each fraction over that denominator by multiplying its numerator and denominator by the same whole number.
Compare the rewritten numerators; the larger numerator gives the larger fraction, and equal numerators mean the fractions are equal.
r18.assess: Which is greater, 5/6 or 7/9? Show your work.
r18.why: Step 1 finds a common multiple of the two denominators, which uses the idea of multiples of a whole number.

r19.statement: Compare two fractions with nonzero numerators by rewriting both with a common numerator; the fraction with the smaller rewritten denominator is greater.
procedure: Find a common multiple of the two numerators (the product of the numerators always works).
Rewrite each fraction with that numerator by multiplying its numerator and denominator by the same whole number.
Compare the rewritten denominators; the smaller denominator gives the larger fraction, and equal denominators mean the fractions are equal.
r19.assess: Which is greater, 2/3 or 3/5? Compare them by making the numerators the same.
r19.why: Step 1 finds a common multiple of the two numerators, which uses multiples of whole numbers.

r20.statement: A decomposition of a/b into groups of parts of size 1/b is recorded as an equation a/b = c/b + d/b + ..., where the numerators on the right add to a.
r20.assess: A model shows 7/5 split into a group of 3 fifths and a group of 4 fifths. Write the equation.
r20.why: The condition that the numerators on the right add to a is a whole-number sum.

r21.statement: Splitting each of the b parts into n equal parts multiplies the number of parts by n and the number of chosen parts by n, while the amount covered does not change; so (n x a)/(n x b) is the same amount as a/b, for every n.
r21.assess: Use a visual fraction model to explain why 2/3 = (4 x 2)/(4 x 3), and say why the same argument works for any n.
r21.why: Counting b parts each split into n parts gives b x n, which equals n x b by the commutative property.

r22.statement: Decide whether two fractions are equivalent by rewriting both over a common denominator with the multiplication principle and comparing numerators.
procedure: Find a common multiple of the two denominators.
Rewrite each fraction over that denominator by multiplying its numerator and denominator by the same whole number.
The fractions are equivalent exactly when the rewritten numerators are equal.
r22.assess: Is 4/6 equivalent to 6/9? Is 6/8 equivalent to 3/5?
r22.why: Step 1 finds a common multiple of the two denominators, such as 18 for 6 and 9.

r23.statement: Estimate a difference of fractions by replacing each fraction with a nearby benchmark (0, 1/2, 1, or a whole number), and use the estimate to judge whether a computed difference is reasonable.
procedure: Replace each fraction with its nearest benchmark: 0, 1/2, 1, or a whole number.
Subtract the benchmarks to get an estimate of the difference.
Call a computed difference unreasonable if it is far from the estimate or is larger than the first fraction.
r23.assess: Jo says 11/12 - 3/8 = 8/4. Use benchmark fractions to decide whether this is reasonable.
r23.why: Step 2 subtracts benchmark whole numbers, for example 2 - 1, to produce the estimate.

r24.statement: Estimate a difference of fractions by replacing each fraction with a nearby benchmark (0, 1/2, 1, or a whole number), and use the estimate to judge whether a computed difference is reasonable.
procedure: Replace each fraction with its nearest benchmark: 0, 1/2, 1, or a whole number.
Subtract the benchmarks to get an estimate of the difference.
Call a computed difference unreasonable if it is far from the estimate or is larger than the first fraction.
r24.assess: Jo says 11/12 - 3/8 = 8/4. Use benchmark fractions to decide whether this is reasonable.
r24.why: Step 2 subtracts benchmark whole numbers, for example 2 - 1, to produce the estimate.

r25.statement: Estimate a sum of fractions by replacing each addend with a nearby benchmark (0, 1/2, 1, or a whole number), and use the estimate to judge whether a computed sum is reasonable.
procedure: Replace each addend with its nearest benchmark: 0, 1/2, 1, or a whole number.
Add the benchmarks to get an estimate of the sum.
Call a computed sum unreasonable if it is far from the estimate or is smaller than one of the addends.
r25.assess: Without computing exactly, decide whether 2/5 + 1/2 = 3/7 can be correct, and explain using benchmark fractions.
r25.why: Step 2 adds benchmark whole numbers, for example 1 + 1, to produce the estimate.

r26.statement: Estimate a sum of fractions by replacing each addend with a nearby benchmark (0, 1/2, 1, or a whole number), and use the estimate to judge whether a computed sum is reasonable.
procedure: Replace each addend with its nearest benchmark: 0, 1/2, 1, or a whole number.
Add the benchmarks to get an estimate of the sum.
Call a computed sum unreasonable if it is far from the estimate or is smaller than one of the addends.
r26.assess: Without computing exactly, decide whether 2/5 + 1/2 = 3/7 can be correct, and explain using benchmark fractions.
r26.why: Step 2 adds benchmark whole numbers, for example 1 + 1, to produce the estimate.

r27.statement: Add two mixed numbers with the same denominator by adding the whole-number parts and the fractional parts separately, regrouping b/b as 1 when the fractional parts sum to 1 or more.
procedure: Add the whole-number parts.
Add the fractional parts by adding numerators over the common denominator b.
If the fractional sum is b/b or more, rewrite it as 1 plus the remaining fraction and add the 1 to the whole-number sum.
Write the whole-number sum and the remaining fraction as a mixed number.
r27.why: Step 1 adds the whole-number parts of the two mixed numbers.

r28.statement: Add two mixed numbers whose fraction parts have unlike denominators by adding whole parts and fraction parts separately over a common denominator, regrouping when the fraction parts sum to 1 or more.
procedure: Rewrite the two fraction parts over a common multiple of their denominators.
Add the fraction parts, and add the whole-number parts.
If the fraction sum is 1 or more, write it as 1 plus a fraction less than 1 and add the 1 to the whole-number sum.
r28.why: Step 1 rewrites the fraction parts over a common multiple of their two denominators.

r29.statement: A decomposition of n a/b into groups of parts of size 1/b is recorded as an equation n a/b = c/b + d/b + ..., where the numerators on the right add to n x b + a.
r29.assess: A model shows 1 3/4 as fourths grouped into 4 fourths, 2 fourths, and 1 fourth. Write the equation.
r29.why: The condition that the numerators on the right add to n x b + a is a whole-number sum, as in fraction.decompose.equation.

r30.statement: Subtract a smaller mixed number from a larger one with the same denominator by subtracting the fractional parts and the whole-number parts separately, first renaming one whole as b/b if the first fractional part is smaller than the second.
procedure: If the fractional part of the first number is smaller than that of the second, rename p a/b as (p - 1) (a + b)/b.
Subtract the fractional numerators over the common denominator b.
Subtract the whole-number parts.
Write the whole-number difference and the fractional difference as a mixed number.
r30.why: Step 3 subtracts the whole-number part of the second number from that of the first.

r31.statement: Subtract a smaller mixed number from a larger one when the fraction parts have unlike denominators by rewriting the fraction parts over a common denominator, regrouping 1 from the whole part when the first fraction part is smaller, then subtracting parts separately.
procedure: Rewrite the two fraction parts over a common multiple n of their denominators.
If the first fraction part is less than the second, take 1 from the first whole part and add n/n to its fraction part.
Subtract the fraction parts, and subtract the whole-number parts.
r31.why: Step 1 rewrites the fraction parts over a common multiple n of their two denominators.

r32.statement: Multiply a fraction or whole number by a fraction by multiplying numerators and multiplying denominators, after writing any whole number q as q/1.
procedure: Write any whole-number factor q as q/1.
Multiply the numerators to get the numerator of the product.
Multiply the denominators to get the denominator of the product.
r32.why: Multiplying the numerators and the denominators are whole-number multiplications that may involve several digits.

r33.statement: For fractions with the same denominator and c no greater than a, a/b - c/b = (a - c)/b.
procedure: Check that the denominators are the same.
Subtract the second numerator from the first.
Write the difference over the common denominator.
r33.why: Step 2 subtracts the second numerator from the first as whole numbers, possibly with several digits.

r34.statement: For fractions with the same denominator and c no greater than a, a/b - c/b = (a - c)/b.
procedure: Check that the denominators are the same.
Subtract the second numerator from the first.
Write the difference over the common denominator.
r34.why: Step 2 subtracts the second numerator from the first as whole numbers, possibly with several digits.

r35.statement: Subtracting one fraction from another means separating the parts of the second from the parts of the first, where both fractions refer to the same whole.
r35.assess: Using one bar as the whole, draw what 4/6 - 1/6 means and say what the difference counts.
r35.why: Subtracting fractions as separating extends the meaning of whole-number subtraction as removing part of an amount.

r36.statement: For a/b at least c/d, find a/b - c/d by rewriting both fractions over a common multiple n of b and d (b x d always works), then subtracting the numerators over n.
procedure: Find a common multiple n of the denominators b and d (b x d is always one).
Rewrite a/b as (a x (n/b))/n and c/d as (c x (n/d))/n.
Subtract the second numerator from the first and write the difference over n.
r36.why: Step 1 finds a common multiple n of the two denominators b and d.

r37.statement: For a/b at least c/d, find a/b - c/d by rewriting both fractions over a common multiple n of b and d (b x d always works), then subtracting the numerators over n.
procedure: Find a common multiple n of the denominators b and d (b x d is always one).
Rewrite a/b as (a x (n/b))/n and c/d as (c x (n/d))/n.
Subtract the second numerator from the first and write the difference over n.
r37.why: Step 2 computes the multiplier n/b and n/d, which are whole-number quotients of the common multiple by each denominator.

r38.statement: For a/b at least c/d, find a/b - c/d by rewriting both fractions over a common multiple n of b and d (b x d always works), then subtracting the numerators over n.
procedure: Find a common multiple n of the denominators b and d (b x d is always one).
Rewrite a/b as (a x (n/b))/n and c/d as (c x (n/d))/n.
Subtract the second numerator from the first and write the difference over n.
r38.why: Alternative route proposed by the critic: Take n = b x d as the common multiple, so the multipliers are d and b and no division or multiples analysis is needed.

r39.statement: A fraction with denominator 10 is rewritten with denominator 100 by multiplying numerator and denominator by 10, so a/10 = (10 x a)/100.
procedure: Multiply the numerator by 10.
Multiply the denominator 10 by 10 to get 100.
Write the result over 100.
r39.assess: Write 7/10 as a fraction with denominator 100.
r39.why: Multiplying the numerator by 10 and forming 10 x 10 = 100 uses base-ten place value.

r40.statement: Find the area of a rectangle with fractional side lengths by rewriting both sides over a common denominator n, tiling the rectangle with squares of side 1/n, and counting squares, each of area 1/(n x n).
procedure: Rewrite both side lengths over a common denominator n, as p/n and q/n.
Tile the rectangle with squares of side 1/n: p along one side and q along the other.
Note that n x n such squares fill a unit square, so each has area 1/(n x n).
Count the p x q squares; the area is (p x q)/(n x n) square units.
r40.assess: A rectangle is 3/4 m by 1/2 m. Tile it with squares of side 1/4 m and find its area.
r40.why: Step 1 needs a common denominator n for the two side lengths, found as a common multiple of the denominators.

r41.statement: For whole numbers a and b, a x b is the total number of objects in a groups with b objects in each group.
r41.assess: In 5 x 7 = 35, counting objects in groups, what does the 5 stand for, what does the 7 stand for, and what does the 35 stand for?
r41.why: The total of a groups with b objects each is found by joining the groups, which is a sum of a equal addends.

r42.statement: Decide whether a product of positive numbers is greater than, equal to, or less than one factor by comparing the other factor with 1, without performing the multiplication.
procedure: Pick the factor q to compare the product with; call the other factor f.
Compare f with 1.
Conclude: the product is greater than q if f > 1, equal to q if f = 1, and less than q if f < 1.
r42.assess: Without multiplying, put these in order from least to greatest: 225, (9/10) x 225, (11/8) x 225.
r42.why: Step 1 may pick either factor as the one to compare against, which uses the commutative property of multiplication.

r43.statement: For a positive number q and a fraction f > 1, write f = 1 + g with g > 0; then q x f = q + q x g, which is q plus a positive amount, so q x f > q. Multiplying by a whole number greater than 1 is the familiar case.
r43.assess: Explain why (5/4) x 12 is greater than 12, and why the same reasoning works for any fraction greater than 1.
r43.why: The step q x (1 + g) = q x 1 + q x g is the distributive property.

r44.statement: For a positive number q and a fraction f > 1, write f = 1 + g with g > 0; then q x f = q + q x g, which is q plus a positive amount, so q x f > q. Multiplying by a whole number greater than 1 is the familiar case.
r44.assess: Explain why (5/4) x 12 is greater than 12, and why the same reasoning works for any fraction greater than 1.
r44.why: The step q x (1 + g) = q x 1 + q x g is the distributive property.

r45.statement: For a positive number q and a fraction f > 1, write f = 1 + g with g > 0; then q x f = q + q x g, which is q plus a positive amount, so q x f > q. Multiplying by a whole number greater than 1 is the familiar case.
r45.assess: Explain why (5/4) x 12 is greater than 12, and why the same reasoning works for any fraction greater than 1.
r45.why: The step q x (1 + g) = q x 1 + q x g is the distributive property.

r46.statement: A problem takes a percent of an original price off as a discount; the learner finds the discount and the resulting sale price.
r46.assess: Shoes that cost $80 are 25% off. What are the discount and the sale price?
r46.why: The sale price is the original minus the discount.

r47.statement: A problem adds one or more percents of a base amount to it, such as a markup, sales tax, or tip; the learner finds each percent of the base and the resulting total.
r47.assess: A meal costs $40. Sales tax is 6% and the tip is 18%, both of the $40. What is the total?
r47.why: Amounts such as $2.40 and $7.20 are decimals that are found and added to the base, as in 40 + 2.4 + 7.2.

r48.statement: A problem gives an original and a new amount; the learner finds the percent change as (new - original)/original x 100, always relative to the original amount.
r48.assess: A price drops from $50 to $40. What is the percent decrease?
r48.why: The difference new - original is the first computation.

r49.statement: A problem gives an original and a new amount; the learner finds the percent change as (new - original)/original x 100, always relative to the original amount.
r49.assess: A price drops from $50 to $40. What is the percent decrease?
r49.why: The difference new - original is the first computation.

r50.statement: A problem gives an original and a new amount; the learner finds the percent change as (new - original)/original x 100, always relative to the original amount.
r50.assess: A price drops from $50 to $40. What is the percent decrease?
r50.why: Computing new - original and dividing by the original, as in 10 divided by 50 equals 0.2, uses decimal arithmetic.

r51.statement: A problem gives an original and a new amount; the learner finds the percent change as (new - original)/original x 100, always relative to the original amount.
r51.assess: A price drops from $50 to $40. What is the percent decrease?
r51.why: The difference new - original is the first computation.

r52.statement: p percent of a quantity Q is (p/100) x Q.
procedure: Write p percent as the rate p/100.
Multiply p/100 by Q.
r52.why: Alternative route proposed by the critic: Decimal route: write p% as a hundredths decimal and multiply by Q

r53.statement: The graph of a proportional relationship y = kx is the line through the origin and the point (1, k).
procedure: Plot (0, 0).
Plot (x, k x x) for one convenient x not 0.
Draw the line through the two points (only the part where both quantities make sense, if the situation restricts them).
r53.assess: Graph y = 2.5x for x from 0 to 4.
r53.why: Graphing y = 2.5x requires computing a point such as (2, 5) by multiplying a decimal slope by x.

r54.statement: The graph of a proportional relationship y = kx is the line through the origin and the point (1, k).
procedure: Plot (0, 0).
Plot (x, k x x) for one convenient x not 0.
Draw the line through the two points (only the part where both quantities make sense, if the situation restricts them).
r54.assess: Graph y = 2.5x for x from 0 to 4.
r54.why: Graphing y = 2.5x requires computing a point such as (2, 5) by multiplying a decimal slope by x.

r55.statement: A problem needs two or more steps of ratio reasoning, such as finding parts from a part-to-part ratio and a total, then comparing or combining them.
r55.assess: The ratio of boys to girls in a class of 32 is 3:5. How many more girls than boys are there?
r55.why: A part-to-part ratio with a total requires adding the parts, such as 3 + 5, to find how many units make the whole.

r56.statement: A problem needs two or more steps of ratio reasoning, such as finding parts from a part-to-part ratio and a total, then comparing or combining them.
r56.assess: The ratio of boys to girls in a class of 32 is 3:5. How many more girls than boys are there?
r56.why: The test problem asks how many more girls than boys, which requires subtracting the two part amounts.

r57.statement: A problem gives a rate as a pair of amounts (cost and items, distance and time, work and time); the learner finds the unit rate and uses it to find another amount at the same rate.
r57.assess: It took 7 hours to mow 4 lawns. At that rate, how many lawns could be mowed in 35 hours, and at what rate were lawns mowed?
r57.why: Using the unit rate to find another amount at the same rate multiplies or divides decimal quantities, as in unit pricing.

r58.statement: Convert a measurement by multiplying it by one or more conversion factors, each written with the unit to remove in the denominator, and cancelling units like common factors.
procedure: Write the measurement with its unit.
Multiply by a conversion factor whose denominator has the current unit and whose numerator has the next unit.
Cancel the matching units and multiply the numbers.
Repeat until the result is in the target unit.
r58.assess: How many inches are in 2.5 yards? (1 yd = 3 ft, 1 ft = 12 in)
r58.why: The test problem 2.5 yards requires multiplying the decimal 2.5 by 3 and then by 12.

r59.statement: A ratio relationship is drawn as two parallel number lines, one per quantity, with aligned tick marks at pairs of values in equivalent ratios, starting from 0 aligned with 0.
r59.assess: A car travels 150 miles on 5 gallons. Use a double number line to find how far it travels on 2 gallons.
r59.why: Finding the distance for 2 gallons from 150 miles on 5 gallons means dividing 150 by 5 to mark 1 gallon.

r60.statement: Compare ratios a:b and c:d by extending both tables to rows with the same value of the first quantity and comparing the values of the second quantity there.
procedure: Make a table of equivalent ratios for each ratio.
Extend both tables until they share a value of the first quantity (a common multiple of a and c always works).
In those rows, the ratio with the larger second value has more of the second quantity per unit of the first.
r60.assess: Mix A uses 3 cups of juice to 5 cups of water; Mix B uses 4 cups of juice to 7 cups of water. Use tables to decide which mix has more water for the same amount of juice.
r60.why: A common multiple of the two first-quantity values guarantees that both tables reach a shared value of the first quantity.

r61.statement: A ratio a:b is drawn as two tapes made of a and b equal-size units; when a total or one quantity is known, dividing it by its number of units gives the unit size.
procedure: Draw a tape of a equal units for the first quantity and a tape of b equal units for the second.
Mark the known amount on the units it covers (one tape, or both tapes for a total).
Divide the known amount by the number of units it covers to get the unit size.
Multiply the unit size by the number of units of the quantity asked for.
r61.assess: The ratio of red to blue marbles is 3:5 and there are 40 marbles. Use a tape diagram to find how many are red.
r61.why: When the known amount is a total, it covers both tapes, so the number of units covered is the sum a + b.

r62.statement: For a ratio a:b with b not 0, the unit rate is a/b: the amount of the first quantity for 1 unit of the second.
r62.assess: The ratio of miles to hours for a trip is 150:4. What is the unit rate, and what does it mean?
r62.why: Finding the unit rate for 150:4 requires dividing 150 by 4 to get the decimal 37.5.

r63.statement: For a ratio a:b with b not 0, the unit rate is a/b: the amount of the first quantity for 1 unit of the second.
r63.assess: The ratio of miles to hours for a trip is 150:4. What is the unit rate, and what does it mean?
r63.why: Finding the unit rate for 150:4 requires dividing 150 by 4 to get the decimal 37.5.

r64.statement: Find the unit rate of a ratio a:b, b not 0, by dividing a by b and naming the result in units of the first quantity per unit of the second.
procedure: Identify the two quantities and which is 'per' which.
Divide the first quantity's value a by the second's value b.
Label the result as units of the first quantity per 1 unit of the second.
r64.assess: A 12-pack of juice costs $9. Find the cost per can.
r64.why: Dividing the first value by the second often gives a decimal result, as in 9 divided by 12 equals 0.75.

r65.statement: For whole numbers with b no greater than a, the difference a - b is the length of the segment from b to a on the number line.
procedure: Locate b and a on the number line.
Measure the length from b up to a, in one jump or in smaller jumps (for example to the next ten, then by tens).
The total length of the jumps is a - b.
r65.assess: Use a number line to find how far it is from 48 to 73, and write the subtraction it shows.
r65.why: The statement says the length of the segment is a - b, so the meaning of subtraction is needed to name that length.

r66.statement: For whole numbers with b no greater than a, the difference a - b is the length of the segment from b to a on the number line.
procedure: Locate b and a on the number line.
Measure the length from b up to a, in one jump or in smaller jumps (for example to the next ten, then by tens).
The total length of the jumps is a - b.
r66.assess: Use a number line to find how far it is from 48 to 73, and write the subtraction it shows.
r66.why: Step 3 adds the lengths of the jumps to get the total distance.

r67.statement: For whole numbers with b no greater than a, the difference a - b is shown by starting at a and moving b units to the left; the point reached is a - b.
procedure: Locate a on the number line.
From a, mark a length of b units to the left, in one jump or in smaller jumps that total b.
Read the label at the endpoint; it is a - b.
r67.assess: Show 62 - 17 on a number line by jumping back from 62, and find the difference.
r67.why: The model represents a - b as what remains when b is taken away from a, so that meaning of subtraction is used.
